introduction: The guide begins by asking whether the object of every Revelation is not to transform the whole character of mankind, and then announces a Divine Springtime in which that change is under way. These readings follow it through their own images: an elixir that turns base metal to gold, sleepers wakened, a second birth, iron made red in the fire, a mirror cleared of rust, growth by stages, the refining of tests, and at last a changed character, which is where the change can be seen. Much of the world’s writing keeps them company. The Gospels and Paul speak of new birth and a new creature, the Qur’an of the dead raised to life and of the earth quickened after her death, Plato of the turning of the whole soul, the Dhammapada of the self as the thing to be conquered. Other voices doubt or resist. Jeremiah asks whether the leopard can change his spots, the Preacher finds nothing new under the sun, Eliot calls April the cruellest month, Polonius commends being true to one’s own self, and Hobbes builds on the wolf that training will not remove. Between them stands the question the readings press: what changes a person, and what part of that is the person’s own doing?
questions: The readings announce a springtime in which all things are made new. Set them beside Ecclesiastes, Eliot’s April and Arnold’s withdrawing sea: what would count as evidence that an age, or a person, has been renewed?
Jeremiah doubts that the leopard can change his spots; Ezekiel promises a heart of flesh for a heart of stone. Where do the readings on the elixir and on iron in the fire stand between them?

The readings on awakening and second birth speak of the heedless as asleep or dead. How do Plato’s turning of the whole soul, Wordsworth’s “sleep and a forgetting” and Nicodemus’s question each picture what a person was before the change?

“Abandon the habitation of self”, the readings say; “to thine own self be true”, says Polonius. Is there a self to be left and a self to be kept, and how do the seed, the grain of wheat and the burning bush help to tell them apart?

The readings treat tests as gain “whatever the deal”. Read them with Job, with Paul to the Romans and with Gloucester’s “flies to wanton boys”. What allows the same suffering to be read so differently?

The closing prayers ask God to purify and remake the one who prays; the Dhammapada answers that no one can purify another, and Aesop that the gods help those who help themselves. How do the readings on capacity and daily effort divide the work?

outside.why: The reading asks whether the object of every Revelation is not “a transformation in the whole character of mankind”. A saying handed down from Muḥammad gives his own mission in the same terms: he was sent to perfect good character.

The reading rests the whole worth of a Revelation on its power to change character. Jeremiah, speaking to a people long accustomed to evil, doubts that habit can be changed any more than skin or spots. What would have to act on a person for the prophet’s question to receive another answer?

“A new springtime arrived … and the birds of the field warbled.” The Song of Solomon has the same season in the same signs, rain over, flowers and birdsong; there a lover uses it to call the beloved out of doors.
The Pen is told to magnify God’s name so “that all created things may be regenerated and made new”. The seer of Patmos hears the same promise from the throne, in six words.

The reading announces a springtime in which all things are made new. The Preacher has watched the seasons return and concludes that nothing under the sun is new. What would distinguish a renewal from one more turn of the year?

The reading tells its hearers to “refresh and revive” their souls in a soul-stirring springtime. Eliot’s poem of 1922 opens by calling the same season cruel, because it stirs dull roots that would rather stay buried. Why might being revived be feared?

“The Sun of Truth hath risen to illumine the whole earth.” The last of the Hebrew prophets promised a Sun of righteousness that would rise with healing in its wings; he promised it to those who fear the Name, and the reading to all peoples.

The reading speaks of a rescue from death and “a new life” bestowed. The Qur’an describes one person in those words, dead and raised to life and given a light to walk by among others, and sets him against one who cannot leave the dark.

The reading foresees the teachings taking “root in the hearts like unto the establishment of the spirit in the souls of men”. Jeremiah looked for the same inward lodging: a law no longer on tablets but written in the heart.

Those who saw the light, says the reading, were so exhilarated that they “forgot the world and their own selves”. Wesley recorded the evening it happened to him, to the quarter-hour: a heart strangely warmed while someone read aloud.

“He has renewed that springtime … the human world has found new life.” Shelley asked the autumn wind to make him the instrument of such a renewal and to drive his dead thoughts over the world “to quicken a new birth”; his is still a prayer, the reading’s a report.

The reading sees the world “advancing and progressing” in a renewed springtime. Arnold, on the beach at Dover, heard the sea of faith withdrawing and found the world without certitude or help for pain. Which signs was each of them reading?

When the clouds of mercy rain on it, the reading says, “this dark earth shall bring forth crimson flowers”. The Qur’an points to the same sight as the print of God’s mercy, the earth quickened after her death, and reasons from it to the raising of the dead.

The reading holds that illnesses of the mind are treated “through the power of the human spirit”, and that the divine spirit rules over both kinds. Macbeth asks a doctor for exactly such a cure and is told that the patient must minister to himself. Where does the reading find the physician the doctor cannot name?

The Prophets appear, says the reading, so “that this lump of coal may become a diamond”. Ezekiel’s promise is of the same change of substance, a stony heart taken out and a heart of flesh given; he moves from hard to soft, the reading from dull to brilliant.

The reading asks for the “Most Great Elixir”, the alchemy that turns the copper and iron of souls to gold. Herbert names the philosophers’ stone too and finds it in a motive: whatever is done as for God is by that touch made gold.

“No man can obtain everlasting life, unless he embraceth the truth of this … Revelation.” The claim has the form of one in John’s Gospel, where no one comes to the Father except by the one who speaks.

The reading allows no everlasting life apart from the one remedy. The Qur’an, in a verse about the communities before it, says that a law and a way were appointed for each, and tells them to compete in good works. How are a single remedy and many appointed ways to be held together?
The prayer asks “that my choice be conformed to Thy choice and my wish to Thy wish”. In Gethsemane the same conforming is prayed at its hardest moment: let this cup pass, yet not as I will.

“Turn your faces from the darkness of estrangement to the effulgent light.” Plato describes education as that turning: the eye cannot go from darkness to light unless the whole body turns, and the soul must turn whole. His light is the good known by reason; the reading’s is unity.

The purpose, says the reading, is that “those who walk in darkness should come into the light”. Isaiah’s words are nearly the same, of a people in the land of the shadow of death on whom light has shined.

The reading hopes its hearers will “bring to life the dead now buried in the graves of their sensual desires”. The Letter to the Ephesians addresses that sleeper directly, in what may be a line of an early hymn: awake, and arise from the dead.

“Thou hast wakened me from my sleep.” Thoreau held that he had never met anyone quite awake and that staying so is the work of a life. The prayer thanks someone for the waking; Thoreau looks for it to an “infinite expectation of the dawn”.

The prayer gives thanks for being wakened and given a desire to perceive what most miss. Wordsworth places the sleep earlier: birth itself is “a sleep and a forgetting” of where the soul came from. Is the awakening in the reading the gaining of something new, or the recovery of something lost?

The prayer remembers “the thirsty ones who have panted after the fountain of Thy living waters”. The psalmist is one of them, and his image has fixed the phrase: the hart panting after the water brooks.
Among the rewards the reading lists: “he was blind and begins to see”. The man healed in John’s Gospel, pressed by examiners, will say only that much, and it is his whole testimony.

The reading recalls Christ’s word that the people are blind, deaf and dumb, and that he will heal them. The passage of Isaiah behind that saying is harsher: the prophet is sent so that ears grow heavy and eyes shut, lest they be healed. What does preaching do to those who will not hear?

“Your cups are filled with choice wine”, the reading says to an assembly, and its Cup-bearer is divine. FitzGerald’s Omar has the wine, the book and the beloved and wants no further paradise than this. How does a reader tell the wine that awakens from the wine that consoles?

The prayer recounts what a people were and what they were made: stilled voices given speech, barren soil made a garden. The Qur’an reminds its first community in the same before-and-after: enemies whose hearts were joined, so that they became brothers.

The life spoken of in the Books of the Prophets “is the life of knowledge”, the recognition of God through His Manifestations. John’s Gospel gives the same definition in a prayer: eternal life is to know God and the one He has sent.

The reading speaks of being “baptized with the Water of Life, with the fire of the love of God and with the Holy Spirit”. The three come from John the Baptist, who sets his own water against a baptism of Spirit and fire still to come.

“From a precious breast ye drew the milk of knowledge, then came ye to your full growth.” The First Letter of Peter uses the same figure for new believers, who are to want the milk of the word in order to grow.

The flower “had a purely mineral life” and through the spring “found another life”; so the reading explains eternal life. Rūmī tells his own ascent by the same steps, from mineral to plant and on, each a death and a rising.
The reading quotes it: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.” Here is the sentence in its place, with the condition that goes before it.

For the reading, material life “is tantamount to non-existence” beside the life of the spirit. The Preacher will not grant the difference so easily: one thing befalls men and beasts, and who knows that the spirit of man goes upward? On what does the reading’s confidence rest?

The reading consoles a family: the one who died was “severed from the garden of the contingent world” and joined to a tree in another. Donne addresses death itself with the same assurance, as one short sleep before an eternal waking.

“The spiritual father is greater than the physical one”, for he gives life everlasting. Paul claims that fatherhood over the Corinthians, having begotten them through the gospel, and distinguishes it from the work of ten thousand instructors.

“Be thou … reborn”, says the reading. When Jesus said as much to a teacher of Israel, the teacher asked the literal question: how can a man be born when he is old? What in a grown person is it that can begin again?

The reading explains the descent of the Holy Spirit as a change in the Apostles, who “were feeble gnats and became soaring eagles”. This is the account it is explaining, with its wind, its tongues of fire and its new speech.

Nightingales are told to leave the thorns for the rose-garden, and friends “that dwell upon the dust” to hasten home. Rūmī’s reed-flute begins his great poem with the same homesickness: cut from the reed-bed, it laments until it returns.

God has kindled a fire “that dieth not”, says the reading, to draw souls upward by the heat of love. The Song of Solomon knows love as that flame, which many waters cannot quench; it is speaking of two lovers.

In the reading the fire of the love of God would melt all the ice of Greenland. Frost’s fire is desire and his ice is hate, and either would do to end the world. What makes one fire a paradise and the other a destruction?

The reading calls its hearer to “abandon the habitation of self and desire … forsake thine own life”. The Gospel puts the same exchange as a paradox: the life that is kept is lost, and the life lost is found.

The reading asks that the habitation of self be abandoned. Polonius, sending his son into the world, gives the opposite rule its best-known form: above all, be true to your own self. Are the two speaking of the same self?
“The seed doth truly sacrifice itself for the tree”: unless it disintegrates, no tree appears. The image is the Gospel’s, where the grain of wheat that does not die remains alone.

Saints “live in the world but are not of it”. An early Christian letter describes a whole community in that way: living in their own countries as sojourners, sharing everything as citizens and enduring everything as foreigners.

The reading recalls Moses seized by the rapture of a Call and turning toward Pharaoh. Exodus tells the call itself: a fire that burns in a bush and does not consume it, and a man who turns aside to look.

The grace of guidance, says the reading, “is like unto the candle which is enkindled in the glass of knowledge”, and the glass is the heart. The image is drawn from the Qur’an’s Verse of Light: a niche, a lamp, the lamp in a glass, light upon light.

The reading calls the world of nature “darkness upon darkness”, lit only from beyond itself. Wordsworth sends his friend out of doors because one impulse from a spring wood teaches more of good and evil than the sages. What does each mean by nature?
“The springs of divine bounty are flowing—drink from them.” Isaiah cries the same invitation in a market-place: everyone who thirsts is to come to the waters and buy without money.

The reading values the fast for what it does within: the heart grows tender and thought is fixed on God. Isaiah’s God asks what a fast does for others, and chooses the one that feeds the hungry and frees the oppressed. How are inward awareness and outward mercy joined in one fast?
“The waters of understanding have washed from thee the stains of remoteness.” The psalmist asks for that washing and for more than washing: a clean heart created, a right spirit renewed.

In the polished mirror “you may behold the Sun in all its fullness”; in the rusted one nothing is reflected, though the sun shines on both. The Beatitude states the same condition without the image: the pure in heart shall see God.

Man “contains all Creation” and is its crowning-point, says the reading. Hamlet can recite that praise, noble in reason and infinite in faculty, and feel none of it: to him man is a quintessence of dust. What has gone out in Hamlet that the reading says must be lit?
“We must endeavor to increase our capacity daily.” The Qur’an swears by the soul and gives the same two outcomes: the one who makes it grow succeeds, and the one who stunts it fails.

That world is one of lights, love and perfections, the reading says, so these must be acquired here, “during this vanishing existence”. Rabbi Jacob’s saying is the same counsel as architecture: this world is the vestibule, and one prepares there for the hall.

The reading traces perfection through the kingdoms, mineral, plant and animal, into the human world. Whitman feels the same stair behind him and counts himself the top of things accomplished and the holder of things to be.
“We must strive unceasingly and without rest” to develop the spiritual nature. Longfellow’s psalm measures a life the same way: each tomorrow should find us farther than today.
The reading asks for tireless effort toward a higher station. A disciple of Confucius shows the daily form of such effort: three questions put to himself every day.

The reading denies that return to this world could perfect anyone: “the renewal of an object’s existence cannot bring about the transformation of its essence”. The Gītā teaches the return it rejects, the spirit changing bodies like garments. What does each say changes when a life is over?

“Active souls and vigilant people rest neither by day nor by night.” Tennyson’s old king has the same impatience with rest: to pause is to rust. He seeks experience for its own sake; the reading’s gardeners work for a forest not their own.

The reading sets out seven steps, through search, love and detachment toward oneness. The Second Letter of Peter has its own ordered ascent, each quality added to the one before, from faith to charity.

With spiritual morals and actions conformed to God’s will, “man has attained the image and likeness of his Creator”. Genesis says that humankind was made so; the reading makes the likeness something attained, and warns of another likeness.

Before maturity, says the reading, a person grasps only what is “superficial and outwardly obvious”; afterwards, the realities of things. Paul marks the same threshold in himself: he spoke and thought as a child, and put childish things away.

The reading sets maturity above childhood: one day after it is worth a year before. The Gospel makes becoming like a little child the condition of entering the kingdom. What in the child is to be outgrown, and what recovered?
“This poison is but sugar and this venom the essence of sweetness.” Shakespeare’s banished duke finds the same in exile: adversity is a venomous toad with a jewel in its head.

Without hard tests, the reading says, “this earthly life would prove barren and vain”. The Qur’an puts it as a question to the believers: did they think they would be left alone on saying “We believe”, and not be tried?
The reading testifies to a countenance “irradiated by adversity”. Job, in the middle of his losses and with no answer yet, says what he expects of them: tried, he will come forth as gold.
“The friends of God shall win and profit under all conditions … Gain is their lot, whatever the deal.” Paul writes the same to the Romans: all things work together for good to those who love God.

The reading is sure that whatever befalls the friends of God is gain. Gloucester, blinded and turned out of doors, draws the other conclusion from suffering: the gods kill us for sport. What is it that lets the same events be read as a wager won?

The reading hopes each hearer will be “more concerned for the interests of others than for your own”. A saying of Muḥammad makes a like measure the test of faith: to wish for one’s brother what one wishes for oneself. The reading asks for a step more.

The reading asks people to put others’ interests before their own. Adam Smith observes that society’s daily business gets done by appeal to each person’s own interest. What part of life can the reading’s hope govern, and what part does Smith describe?

“Until man acquires perfections himself, he will not be able to teach perfections to others.” The Dhammapada gives the same order of work: direct yourself first, then teach; make yourself what you tell others to be.

“Every universal cause is divine and every particular one is temporal”, says the reading, and it asks for service to the whole race. Marcus Aurelius has the principle in a line: what does not benefit the hive does not benefit the bee.

“Confine thy thoughts to whatever will lift up the human soul.” The Dhammapada opens with the reason: all that we are is the result of what we have thought, and pain follows an evil thought as the wheel follows the ox.
“Strive with your own selves—this indeed is the greater striving.” The Dhammapada ranks the victories in the same order: to conquer oneself is more than to conquer a thousand thousand in battle.

The reading is asked whether those who do good and wish all people well have any need of divine teachings, and answers that their deeds alone are not sufficient. Paine speaks for those people: he professes no church’s creed, and his own mind is his church. What does the reading say such a person lacks?

Good works are praiseworthy, the reading says, “but these actions alone are not sufficient”. The Letter to the Ephesians had drawn the same line more sharply: salvation is a gift through faith, and not of works.

There is a vast difference, the reading says, between one “who merely reads the words” and one “who tries to live them”. James says it of hearers and doers, with a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his own face.
“When he returned Gregory was quite another Gregory. He had become a new creation.” The phrase is Paul’s: anyone in Christ is a new creature, old things passed away.

Souls are to be trained “until these frenzied beasts change to gazelles … and these wolves to lambs of God”. Isaiah saw the wolf dwelling with the lamb; the reading turns his vision of the animals into a task of education.

The reading expects training to turn wolves into lambs. Hobbes grants both sayings, that man is a god to man and a wolf to man, and builds a state on the second, to restrain what he does not expect to change. Is the wolf educated out of us, or only governed?

Children are fostered and educated, the reading says, “so that they may develop along every line”. The proverb states the trust behind every such school: train a child in the way, and the grown person will not leave it.
“We are as plants, and Thy bounty is as the rain; refresh and cause these plants to grow.” Hopkins ends a sonnet of complaint with the same prayer in four words: send my roots rain.
The prayer asks that a sapling be made “verdant, fresh and flourishing”. The first psalm’s tree is planted by the rivers, bears in season, and its leaf does not wither.
“Think not of your own limitations.” Paul, who had asked three times to be rid of his, records the answer he was given: grace is sufficient, and strength is made perfect in weakness.

The reading calls for lute and harp, viol and lyre, so that east and west are “filled with exceeding joy”. The last psalm is such an orchestra, trumpet, harp, timbrel and cymbals, and everything that has breath.
The songs of fellowship are to carry away “the people of east and west” with gladness. Schiller’s hymn to joy claims the same power for it: under its gentle reign all mankind are brethren.

The prayer is that each may “shine as a radiant star in the dark places of the world”. Portia, coming home at night, sees one candle in her hall and makes the comparison herself: so shines a good deed in a naughty world.

The reading expects its hearer to “raise the banner of peace” and awaken souls. The Gospel warns what an awakening can cost at first: not peace but a sword, and a household divided. What peace lies on the far side of that division?
“By the light of Thy glory reveal unto me Thy path.” The opening chapter of the Qur’an, said in every daily prayer, asks the same: show us the straight path.

The prayer asks to be confirmed and shown the way. Aesop’s waggoner prays from his knees beside a stuck wheel and is told to put his shoulder to it. What does a prayer for transformation leave for the one who prays to do?
The prayer asks for “living waters” that free whoever drinks from attachment to anything else. The water offered at the well in Samaria works the same change: whoever drinks it does not thirst again.

The prayer is to be rid of attachment, not to be given what one is attached to. Marcus Aurelius recommends exactly that turn: where another prays to be released from a thing, pray not to desire the release.
“Deliver me from darkness, make me a brilliant light.” An Upanishad’s prayer moves the same way: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.
The prayer commends souls who “bound their hearts to Thee” and were illumined. The Qur’an speaks of such friends of God as those on whom no fear comes, and who do not grieve.

The prayer asks for help “to turn my face towards Thy face, to fix mine eyes upon Thee”. Augustine begins his Confessions with why a creature would ask it: the heart is made for God and is restless until it rests there.
The prayer asks God to send what will purify the one who prays, “that I may be worthy to praise Thee”. Augustine prayed in the same logic: give what You command, and command what You will.
The prayer asks to be purified “of all that is not of Thee”. Donne asks more violently for the same remaking: knocking and mending are not enough, and he must be broken and made new.

The prayer asks that purity be sent down from the clouds of mercy. The Dhammapada says that purity and impurity belong to oneself and that “no one can purify another”. What does the one who prays for purity still have to do?

jeremiah-leopard-spots.text: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil

song-winter-is-past.text: For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land

revelation-all-things-new.text: And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new

ezekiel-heart-of-flesh.text: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh

john-way-truth-life.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me

isaiah-great-light.text: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined

ephesians-awake-thou.text: Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light

psalm-hart-panteth.text: As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God

john-blind-now-i-see.text: He answered and said, Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see

isaiah-ears-heavy.text: And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed

john-life-eternal-know.text: And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent

matthew-baptize-with-fire.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire

peter-newborn-babes.text: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby

corinthians-not-many-fathers.text: For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel

john-nicodemus.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born

acts-pentecost.text: And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance

song-strong-as-death.text: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it

matthew-lose-his-life.text: For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it

john-corn-of-wheat.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit

exodus-burning-bush.text: And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt. And when the Lord saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush, and said, Moses, Moses. And he said, Here am I

isaiah-come-to-the-waters.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price

matthew-pure-in-heart.text: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God

corinthians-childish-things.text: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things

matthew-as-little-children.text: Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven

job-come-forth-as-gold.text: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold

romans-all-things-work-together.text: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose

corinthians-new-creature.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new

corinthians-strength-in-weakness.text: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness

psalm-trumpet-and-harp.text: Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals. Let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. Praise ye the Lord

quran-dead-raised-to-life.text: Is he who was dead and We have raised him unto life, and set for him a light wherein he walketh among men, as him whose similitude is in utter darkness whence he cannot emerge? Thus is their conduct made fairseeming for the disbelievers.

quran-earth-after-her-death.text: Look, therefore, at the prints of Allah's mercy (in creation): how He quickeneth the earth after her death. Lo! He verily is the Quickener of the Dead, and He is Able to do all things.

quran-left-untested.text: Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction?

quran-light-verse.text: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is as it were a shining star. (This lamp is) kindled from a blessed tree, an olive neither of the East nor of the West, whose oil would almost glow forth (of itself) though no fire touched it. Light upon light

quran-soul-grow-or-stunt.text: And a soul and Him Who perfected it And inspired it (with conscience of) what is wrong for it and (what is) right for it. He is indeed successful who causeth it to grow, And he is indeed a failure who stunteth it

eliot-cruellest-month.text: April is the cruellest month, breeding / Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing / Memory and desire, stirring / Dull roots with spring rain
eliot-cruellest-month.author: T. S. Eliot
eliot-cruellest-month.locator: I. The Burial of the Dead, lines 1–4

donne-batter-my-heart.text: Batter my heart, three-person'd God; for you / As yet but knock; breathe, shine, and seek to mend; / That I may rise, and stand, o'erthrow me, and bend / Your force, to break, blow, burn, and make me new … Take me to you, imprison me, for I, / Except you enthrall me, never shall be free, / Nor ever chaste, except you ravish me
donne-batter-my-heart.author: John Donne

frost-fire-and-ice.text: Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice. / From what I’ve tasted of desire / I hold with those who favor fire. / But if it had to perish twice, / I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great / And would suffice
frost-fire-and-ice.author: Robert Frost

wordsworth-vernal-wood.text: One impulse from a vernal wood / May teach you more of man; / Of moral evil and of good, / Than all the sages can
wordsworth-vernal-wood.author: William Wordsworth

longfellow-farther-than-today.text: Not enjoyment, and not sorrow, / Is our destined end or way; / But to act, that each to-morrow / Find us farther than to-day
longfellow-farther-than-today.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

tennyson-ulysses.text: How dull it is to pause, to make an end, / To rust unburnish'd, not to shine in use! / As tho' to breathe were life
tennyson-ulysses.author: Alfred Tennyson

dhammapada-what-we-have-thought.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage

gita-worn-out-robes.text: Nay, but as when one layeth / His worn-out robes away, / And, taking new ones, sayeth, / "These will I wear to-day!" / So putteth by the spirit / Lightly its garb of flesh, / And passeth to inherit / A residence afresh
gita-worn-out-robes.locator: 2.22, in Edwin Arnold’s verse (The Song Celestial)

khayyam-jug-of-wine.text: A Book of Verses underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread—and Thou / Beside me singing in the Wilderness— / Oh, Wilderness were Paradise enow
khayyam-jug-of-wine.author: Omar Khayyám
khayyam-jug-of-wine.locator: quatrain 12 in Edward FitzGerald’s fifth edition

herbert-famous-stone.text: This is the famous stone / That turneth all to gold: / For that which God doth touch and own / Cannot for lesse be told
herbert-famous-stone.author: George Herbert

dhammapada-direct-himself-first.text: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer. If a man make himself as he teaches others to be, then, being himself well subdued, he may subdue (others); one's own self is indeed difficult to subdue

plato-turning-of-the-soul.text: our argument shows that the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being, and learn by degrees to endure the sight of being, and of the brightest and best of being, or in other words, of the good
plato-turning-of-the-soul.author: Plato

shakespeare-mind-diseased.text: Canst thou not minister to a mind diseased, / Pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow, / Raze out the written troubles of the brain / And with some sweet oblivious antidote / Cleanse the stuff'd bosom of that perilous stuff / Which weighs upon the heart? / Therein the patient / Must minister to himself
shakespeare-mind-diseased.author: William Shakespeare

shakespeare-flies-to-wanton-boys.text: As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods. / They kill us for their sport
shakespeare-flies-to-wanton-boys.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-thine-own-self.text: This above all: to thine ownself be true, / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man
shakespeare-thine-own-self.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-little-candle.text: How far that little candle throws his beams! / So shines a good deed in a naughty world
shakespeare-little-candle.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

avot-vestibule.text: Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY licence.

donne-death-be-not-proud.text: Death be not proud, though some have callèd thee / Mighty and dreadfull, for, thou art not so … One short sleepe past, wee wake eternally, / And death shall be no more, death, thou shalt die
donne-death-be-not-proud.author: John Donne
